skill.title: Testing
skill.summary: Test design, fixtures, test doubles and keeping a suite trustworthy.
skill.description: Write tests that catch regressions without slowing teams down: choosing cases, using fixtures and mocks correctly, and diagnosing flaky tests.

questions.title: Default fixture scope
questions.prompt: A pytest fixture is declared with `@pytest.fixture` and no arguments. How often is it set up?

options.text: Once per test function that requests it
Once per module
Once per test session
Once per test, even for tests that don't request it

questions.explanation: The default scope is `function`: each test that requests the fixture gets a fresh instance, which keeps tests isolated. Broader scopes (`module`, `session`) trade isolation for speed and should be used for expensive, read-only resources.
rubric: Identifies `function` as the default scope.
Explains that fixtures run only for tests that request them (unless `autouse`).
Describes the isolation versus speed trade-off of wider scopes.
misconceptions: Fixtures are shared across a module by default.
Every fixture runs for every test.
questions.acceptance_criteria: States that the default fixture scope is function.

questions.title: Choosing test cases
questions.prompt: `apply_discount(price: Decimal, percent: int) -> Decimal` returns the discounted price rounded to two decimal places, and should reject invalid percentages. List the test cases you would write and say what each one protects against.
questions.hint: Think about typical values, boundaries, invalid input and rounding.
questions.explanation: Good coverage includes a typical case, the boundaries (0% and 100%), just outside them (-1%, 101%) expecting errors, rounding behaviour at half-cent values, a zero price, and the use of `Decimal` rather than float. Each test should state one behaviour so failures are easy to read.
rubric: Includes at least one typical, representative case.
Tests boundaries at 0% and 100%.
Tests invalid inputs outside the allowed range and the expected error.
Tests rounding behaviour explicitly.
Explains what regression each case would catch.
misconceptions: One happy-path test is enough for a small function.
Line coverage proves the function is correct.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Covers typical, boundary, invalid and rounding cases and says what each protects against.

questions.title: Patching the wrong name
questions.prompt: `app/service.py` contains `from app.clients import fetch_rate` and calls `fetch_rate()` inside `convert()`. A test wraps `convert()` in `mock.patch("app.clients.fetch_rate")`. What happens?

options.text: `convert()` uses the mock, because the patch replaces the function everywhere
`convert()` still calls the real `fetch_rate`; patch `app.service.fetch_rate` instead
The test errors because `app.clients.fetch_rate` cannot be patched
It works only if the test imports `app.service` after applying the patch

questions.explanation: `from ... import` binds a second name, `fetch_rate`, in `app.service`'s namespace at import time. Patching `app.clients.fetch_rate` rebinds only the original name. Patch where the name is looked up: `app.service.fetch_rate`.
rubric: Explains that `from x import y` creates a separate binding in the importing module.
States that `mock.patch` replaces a name in one namespace only.
Patches the name where it is looked up.
misconceptions: Patching a function replaces it in every module.
Import order alone determines whether a patch applies.

resources.title: Python docs: unittest.mock — Where to patch

questions.acceptance_criteria: Explains the real function is still called and patches the name where it is looked up.

questions.title: Investigating a flaky test
questions.prompt: A test passes locally but fails about one time in twenty in CI. Describe how you would investigate it, the most common root causes of flaky tests, and what you would do while the root cause is still unknown.
questions.hint: Make the failure reproducible before trying to fix it.
questions.explanation: Reproduce first: run the test repeatedly, alone and with the full suite, with randomised order, and compare CI and local environments. Common causes are shared state between tests, time and timezone dependence, ordering assumptions, real network calls or timers, and concurrency. While investigating, quarantine with a tracked ticket rather than deleting it or silently retrying.
rubric: Reproduces the failure by repeated and randomised runs before changing code.
Lists several common causes: shared state, time, ordering, network, concurrency.
Uses CI logs and environment differences as evidence.
Quarantines with a tracked owner instead of deleting or silently retrying.
Fixes the root cause and guards against recurrence.
misconceptions: Automatic retries fix flaky tests.
A test that passes locally must be correct.

resources.title: Martin Fowler: Eradicating non-determinism in tests

questions.acceptance_criteria: Reproduces the failure before fixing, lists several real causes, and quarantines rather than silently retrying.

questions.title: A test strategy for an API with dependencies
questions.prompt: A FastAPI service stores data in PostgreSQL and charges cards through a third-party payment provider. Design its test strategy: what you test at each level, how you treat the database and the payment provider, and how you keep the suite fast and trustworthy.
questions.hint: Which fakes could disagree with reality without any test noticing?
questions.explanation: Unit-test pure domain logic without I/O. Run API and repository tests against a real PostgreSQL (e.g. a container) because SQLite or mocks hide constraint, type and locking behaviour. Put the payment provider behind an interface you own; test against a fake in most tests, verify the adapter against the provider's sandbox or recorded contract, and add a few end-to-end smoke tests. Keep tests isolated with per-test transactions or truncation, and run slow suites in parallel or less often.
rubric: Separates fast unit tests of domain logic from integration tests.
Uses a real PostgreSQL for persistence tests and explains why substitutes mislead.
Wraps the payment provider behind an owned interface with a fake for most tests.
Verifies the real integration via contract tests or the provider's sandbox.
Addresses isolation, data setup and suite speed.
misconceptions: Mocking everything gives the most reliable suite.
SQLite is an adequate stand-in for PostgreSQL in tests.

resources.title: Martin Fowler: The practical test pyramid

questions.acceptance_criteria: Separates unit and integration levels, uses real PostgreSQL, and isolates the payment provider behind an owned interface verified by contract or sandbox tests.

questions.title: A timestamp test that fails sometimes
questions.prompt: This test passes most of the time but occasionally fails in CI. Why?
questions.hint: How many times is the clock read, and when?

options.text: `datetime.now()` is called twice, at slightly different moments
pytest runs assertions before the function under test returns
`datetime` objects cannot be compared with `==`
CI machines do not have a system clock

questions.explanation: The function reads the clock once and the test reads it again a little later. Usually both fall within the same microsecond or the comparison is lucky, but sometimes they differ and the test fails. Make time an input: pass a clock or `now` into the function, or freeze time in the test, and assert against that fixed value.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “datetime.now()` is called twice, at slightly different moments”. The function reads the clock once and the test reads it again a little later.
rubric: Identifies the two separate clock reads.
Explains why the failure is intermittent.
Proposes injecting a clock or freezing time.
misconceptions: Fast code makes timing differences impossible.
Flaky tests are caused by the CI system, not the test.

resources.title: Martin Fowler: Eradicating non-determinism in tests

questions.title: A refactor that breaks a test
questions.prompt: `fetch_rate()` was rewritten to use `httpx` instead of `requests`. It returns exactly the same values, but this test now fails. What is the underlying problem?
questions.hint: Did the behaviour that users depend on change?

options.text: `httpx` is incompatible with `unittest.mock`
The test is coupled to implementation details instead of observable behaviour
The mock should be configured with `side_effect` instead of `return_value`
Mocks must be reset between tests, and this one leaked state

questions.explanation: The test asserts which library is called and how, so any internal change breaks it even when behaviour is correct. Tests should check outcomes at a boundary you own: put HTTP behind your own client interface and use a fake in unit tests, or stub responses at the transport level, and assert on what `fetch_rate` returns. Reserve interaction assertions for interactions that are part of the contract.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “The test is coupled to implementation details instead of observable behaviour”. The test asserts which library is called and how, so any internal change breaks it even when behaviour is correct.
rubric: Identifies over-specification / coupling to implementation.
Proposes asserting on observable results.
Proposes a boundary you own with a fake or stub.
misconceptions: More interaction assertions make tests stronger.
Mocks should mirror every internal call.

questions.title: High coverage, missed bug
questions.prompt: A pricing module has 95% line coverage, yet a change from `>=` to `>` in a discount threshold shipped without any test failing. Which technique would most directly reveal that the tests are too weak?
questions.hint: Would any existing test fail if the operator changed?

options.text: Raising the coverage requirement to 100% of lines
Mutation testing, which checks whether small code changes make tests fail
Snapshot tests that store the full output of each function
Running the existing suite in random order on every build

questions.explanation: Coverage shows that lines ran, not that assertions would notice them being wrong. Mutation testing makes small changes such as `>=` to `>` and reports mutants that no test catches, which points straight at missing boundary assertions. Here, a test exactly at the threshold would kill that mutant. Mutation testing is slower, so it is usually run on critical modules or changed files.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “Mutation testing, which checks whether small code changes make tests fail”. Coverage shows that lines ran, not that assertions would notice them being wrong.
rubric: Explains that coverage measures execution, not assertion strength.
Chooses mutation testing and explains surviving mutants.
Identifies the missing boundary test.
Mentions the runtime cost and targeted use.
misconceptions: High coverage means good tests.
Snapshot tests catch logic errors automatically.

resources.title: Stryker docs: What is mutation testing?

questions.title: Both suites green, production broken
questions.prompt: The orders service renamed a JSON field from `total` to `amount`. Its own tests passed, and the billing service's tests (which mock the orders API) also passed. Billing then broke in production. What would most directly have caught this before release?
questions.hint: Where does billing's assumption about the field name live, and who checks it?

options.text: More unit tests inside the orders service
Consumer-driven contract tests verified against the orders service in its pipeline
Longer end-to-end tests in a shared staging environment run once a week
Raising code coverage in the billing service

questions.explanation: Each suite tested against its own assumptions: billing's mocks still returned `total`. A consumer-driven contract records what billing actually relies on and is verified against the real orders service on every change, so the rename fails the orders pipeline immediately. End-to-end tests can catch it too, but they are slow, flaky and run late.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “Consumer-driven contract tests verified against the orders service in its pipeline”. Each suite tested against its own assumptions: billing's mocks still returned `total`.
rubric: Explains why mocks let each side drift.
Chooses consumer-driven contract tests run in the provider's pipeline.
Compares with end-to-end tests on speed and feedback time.
misconceptions: Mocks of other services stay accurate on their own.
End-to-end tests are the only way to test integrations.

questions.title: A test that never ran
questions.prompt: This file is `tests/test_cart.py`. The suite passes, but the bug in `total` is real. Why did pytest not catch it?
questions.hint: Which function names does pytest collect?

options.text: pytest only runs tests marked with `@pytest.mark.test` or listed in `pytest.ini`
pytest collects functions whose names start with `test`; this one is never collected
Plain `assert` statements are stripped unless pytest runs with the `-O` flag
pytest skips any test function that does not request at least one fixture

questions.explanation: By default pytest collects functions whose names start with `test` in files named `test_*.py` or `*_test.py`. `check_total` does not match, so it was never run, and an empty run looks green. Rename it `test_total`, and watch for a test count that does not change when you add tests.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “pytest collects functions whose names start with `test`; this one is never collected”. By default pytest collects functions whose names start with `test` in files named `test_*.py` or `*_test.py`.
rubric: Identifies the naming convention for test functions.
Explains that an uncollected test silently passes.
Proposes renaming and checking the collected count.
misconceptions: Any function in a test file is a test.
A green suite means every test ran.

resources.title: pytest docs: Conventions for Python test discovery

questions.title: Passes alone, fails in the suite
questions.prompt: `test_b` passes when run on its own but fails when the whole file runs. What is the cause?
questions.hint: What does `test_b` see if `test_a` ran first?

options.text: pytest runs tests in parallel by default
`test_a` mutates module-level state that `test_b` depends on
`test_b` needs a `@pytest.mark.order` marker
Assertions in the first test disable the second

questions.explanation: `REGISTRY` is a module-level list shared by every test in the process. `test_a` appends to it, so when `test_b` runs afterwards the list is not empty. Tests must not depend on order: create fresh state in a fixture (or reset it with `monkeypatch`), so each test starts from a known baseline. Running tests in random order (for example with `pytest-randomly`) exposes these dependencies.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “test_a` mutates module-level state that `test_b` depends on”. `REGISTRY` is a module-level list shared by every test in the process.
rubric: Identifies shared module-level state.
Explains the order dependency.
Proposes fixtures or monkeypatch for fresh state.
Suggests random ordering to detect it.
misconceptions: Tests run in isolated processes by default.
Fixing the order is a valid solution.

questions.title: A mock that accepts anything
questions.prompt: `send_email(to, subject, body)` was renamed `send_email(recipient, subject, body)`, and production calls with `to=` started failing. The unit test still passes. Why, and what would have caught it?
questions.code:
from unittest.mock import patch

def test_notifies_owner():
    with patch("app.notify.send_email") as send:
        notify_owner(order)
        send.assert_called_once_with(to="a@b.c", subject="Paid", body=ANY)
questions.hint: What does a default MagicMock do with unexpected keyword arguments?

options.text: pytest cached the old function object; clearing `.pytest_cache` would have caught it
A plain mock accepts any arguments; `autospec=True` enforces the real signature
`assert_called_once_with` only checks how many calls were made, not their arguments
`patch` stops replacing a function once its parameters are renamed in the source

questions.explanation: `patch` replaces the function with a `MagicMock` that accepts any call, so `send_email(to=...)` succeeds in the test even though the real function no longer takes `to`. `patch(..., autospec=True)` (or `create_autospec`) builds a mock with the real signature, so the wrong keyword raises `TypeError` in the test. Integration or contract tests catch the rest.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “A plain mock accepts any arguments; `autospec=True` enforces the real signature”. `patch` replaces the function with a `MagicMock` that accepts any call, so `send_email(to=...)` succeeds in the test even though the real function no longer takes `to`.
rubric: Explains that plain mocks accept any arguments.
Proposes autospec to enforce signatures.
Mentions integration tests as a complement.
misconceptions: A passing mock-based test proves the call is valid.
Mocks check signatures by default.
